name: Leftwards Hand
baseMeaning: Shows an open hand held out sideways, palm turned toward the left.
tldr: 🫲 Leftwards Hand — handing something over, or receiving it.

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as handing something over, or receiving it.
contextMeanings.example: Asking someone to pass the salt back 🫲

contextMeanings.meaning: Used sarcastically it is the gesture with the deadpan delivery: handing something over, or receiving it, said without believing any of it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — handing something over, or receiving it — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: an open hand held out sideways, palm turned toward the left. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Offering a ride or a seat to a friend 🫲

platformNotes.note: WhatsApp renders 🫲 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the hands section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like asking someone to pass the salt back.

On Instagram 🫲 usually arrives as the tail of a caption rather than as a post of its own — a sign-off that reads as handing something over, or receiving it under a photo, or a reaction somebody left on a story.

In TikTok comments 🫲 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays handing something over, or receiving it, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🫲 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for offering a ride or a seat to a friend, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🫲 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its handing something over, or receiving it reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

generationalNotes.note: Millennials tend to send 🫲 deliberately, usually for something like asking someone to pass the salt back, and they read handing something over, or receiving it into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🫲 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read handing something over, or receiving it into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🫲 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the handing something over, or receiving it subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for 🫲 to do the work of offering a ride or a seat to a friend, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is handing something over, or receiving it.

warnings.title: 🫲 and 🫱 get swapped
warnings.description: The Rightwards Hand 🫱 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the two are mirror images that some keyboards swap, so the direction sent may not be the one shown. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🫲 as something else fairly often: it gets swapped for a pointing hand when the sender wants to show where something is, since both push the eye leftward and look similar at small sizes. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 🫲 Leftwards Hand Emoji: Meaning, Uses and Common Misreads
seoDescription: 🫲 Leftwards Hand explained: what the drawing shows, when people send it, and why it gets misread as something else.

longForm.overview:
The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets swapped for a pointing hand when the sender wants to show where something is, since both push the eye leftward and look similar at small sizes. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🫱 Rightwards Hand: the two are mirror images that some keyboards swap, so the direction sent may not be the one shown. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

Five other pages sit under this one. The leftwards hand comes in light, medium-light, medium, medium-dark and dark, and each one is written from the point of view of the person who picked that swatch. The drawing is identical in all five; only the tone moves.

So: what is the leftwards hand for? Mostly offering a ride or a seat to a friend, and then asking someone to pass the salt back. The rest of this page covers the drawing, the second reading it invites, and the tone variants, which are written as separate pages because they are read differently.

Start with the drawing: 🫲 is an open hand held out sideways, palm turned toward the left. It came into the emoji set in Unicode 14.0, under the hands heading, and it has been doing one job ever since — standing in for a sentence the sender did not want to type.

That job is handing something over, or receiving it. It is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture carries the same weight as the sentence it replaces, which is why it lands faster than a sentence would have.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Rooms change the meaning. 🫲 sent to a colleague is a piece of work, 🫲 sent to a friend is a joke, and 🫲 sent to somebody you are seeing is a small dare. Nobody reads it out of context, and that is exactly why the same emoji is not the same message in each of those threads.

The tone does the same job in a different register: the five variants of this emoji carry the identical gesture, and the swatch is a quiet statement about the sender.

Worth watching: how often 🫲 arrives as the entire answer to a question. The sender saves themselves a sentence, and the sentence was where the actual thought was. By the time it reaches the reader, all that is left is a drawing that reads as "handing something over, or receiving it" for some people and as something else for others.

Two jobs, most of the time. The first is offering a ride or a seat to a friend: the emoji goes at the end of a line that has already made the point, and it saves the sender from explaining how they want it taken. The second is asking someone to pass the salt back, and there it is not the punchline but the tone — the message would survive without it, but it would read as flat.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
The riskiest use is the one where the picture carries a message the words were carrying better. 🫲 gets swapped for a pointing hand when the sender wants to show where something is, since both push the eye leftward and look similar at small sizes, and once the emoji is doing the work the message has drifted somewhere neither side intended.

First exchanges are worse. There is no warmth in the drawing, and leftwards hand gestures collect a slightly superior edge from years of being used as answers to other people's messages.

And leave it out of the rooms where the tone is supposed to be level. 🫲 in a thread about somebody's work, or sent to a client you have not met, says very little and can read as handing something over, or receiving it — which sounds like arrogance in a place where arrogance is expensive.

The first thing to check is whether you meant 🫱 Rightwards Hand. The two are mirror images that some keyboards swap, so the direction sent may not be the one shown. Those two are close in every picker, and the wrong one does not soften the message, it changes it.

The second thing to check is whose thread it is. 🫲 sent as a reaction to somebody who is upset reads as handing something over, or receiving it, and the picture is about the gesture rather than about them.
longForm.howToReply:
Unsure? Answer the sentence, not the picture. 🫲 gets swapped for a pointing hand when the sender wants to show where something is, since both push the eye leftward and look similar at small sizes, and the words around it are the only thing that tells you which reading you are in.

For warmth without the ambiguity, write the line as well as sending the picture. A message like offering a ride or a seat to a friend needs the sentence: the drawing alone leaves the reader deciding between handing something over, or receiving it and something sharper.

Reply with 🫲 itself when the message was a reaction. It confirms the tone and adds nothing, which is what a reaction deserves.

But when 🫲 was pointed at you, do not answer with a picture. A nudge, a handover, a request for a decision — those need a sentence, because a gesture answering a gesture leaves the point unanswered.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🫲 and 🫱?
faqs.answer: The two are mirror images that some keyboards swap, so the direction sent may not be the one shown. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🫲 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as handing something over, or receiving it, but it gets swapped for a pointing hand when the sender wants to show where something is, since both push the eye leftward and look similar at small sizes. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🫲 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🫲 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under leftwards hand show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🫲 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🫲 is used for handing something over, or receiving it. The drawing shows an open hand held out sideways, palm turned toward the left, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

conversationExamples.message: asking someone to pass the salt back 🫲
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as handing something over, or receiving it, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🫲
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets swapped for a pointing hand when the sender wants to show where something is, since both push the eye leftward and look similar at small sizes more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: offering a ride or a seat to a friend 🫲
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is handing something over, or receiving it, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: offering a ride or a seat to a friend 🫲
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as handing something over, or receiving it, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.
